I read all 20 files in full with line numbers, top-level script code included. I also checked two pieces of context. The ecommerce webapp's `templates/` and `static/` folders never mention `trace`, so the trace output it asks Vespa for is unused. The book schema holds only the five fields the page displays, so `select *` there costs nothing extra. The raw Instacart and Amazon input files are not in the checkout, so I did not measure any of these leads. "Impact" below is my estimate from the code alone.

## examples/workshop-ecommerce/preprocess.py
All of these need the Instacart CSVs, but a small synthetic CSV would work. No network except the download function.

1. **`check_and_download_dataset`, L84–92.** The download is read in 8192-byte chunks. For every chunk it formats `percent` and calls `print(..., flush=True)`, so a large zip causes tens of thousands of terminal flushes. A larger `chunk_size` or printing only when the whole percent changes would remove most of them. Impact is low. Needs network.
2. **`process_products`, L139–146 and L152–165.** It reads all three CSVs and merges the full product table, even though the default run (`limit=10`) writes only 10 rows. Trimming `df_products` to `.head(limit)` before the merge would avoid this. L152 then uses `iterrows()`, which builds a pandas Series per row. `itertuples()` or `to_dict("records")` would be cheaper. L154 and L156 read `product['product_id']` twice.
3. **`process_users`, L175–185.** It reads all of `orders.csv` and keeps every column, though only `order_id`, `user_id`, `order_dow` and `order_hour_of_day` are used (`usecols` would drop the rest). It then merges and groups the whole dataset. In sample mode that is all done to write 10 users.
4. **`process_users`, L202–209.** It calls `iterrows()` on every purchase row of every user, building one Series per row and four scalar lookups plus `int()` on each. This is the hottest loop in the file. `user_purchases_df[[...]].astype(int).to_dict("records")` gives the same dicts. L212 and L214 each compute `int(user_id)`.
5. **`process_orders`, L234.** It reads `orders.csv` again, after `process_users` already read it in the same run (`main`, L401 then L412). Reading it once and passing the DataFrame would save a full CSV parse.
6. **`process_orders`, L238.** `.copy()` on a frame produced by boolean indexing is an extra full copy. The frame is only merged afterwards, never changed in place.
7. **`process_orders`, L253–262.** It sorts all of `order_products` and then aggregates with a Python `lambda x: list(x)` per group. `.agg(list)` or a groupby without the lambda is cheaper. As in item 3, the full sort, groupby and merge (L270) all run even when only `limit` rows are written.
8. **`process_orders`, L290–302.** `iterrows()` again. L299–300 reads `order["days_since_prior_order"]` twice per row.

## examples/ecommerce-user-preferences/webapp/app.py
This file depends on network calls to OpenAI, Vespa and Wikipedia. `load_system_prompt` and the query-building parts of `query_vespa` and `query_vespa_facets` are pure-ish.

9. **`load_system_prompt`, L46–49, called from `chat` at L435.** `system_prompt.txt` is opened and read from disk on every `/api/chat` request. It could be read once when the module loads.
10. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L86, 96, 118, 146, 179.** Every call is a bare `requests.get` with no shared `Session`, so each one opens a new TCP and TLS connection to en.wikipedia.org. A single lookup can make three or more of these calls.
11. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L133–163.** It makes one sequential `imageinfo` HTTP request per matching image. The MediaWiki API accepts several titles joined with `|`, so one request could cover all of them.
12. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L167–196.** The fallback loop asks again for the same images the first loop already queried, whenever they match a keyword but returned no URL and are not .svg/.png/.gif. It also recomputes `image.get("title","").lower()`.
13. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L103, 127, 208 (failures are not cached).** When no image is found it returns `None` without writing to `IMAGE_CACHE`. Every later request for that make and model repeats the whole Wikipedia sequence, two to N+3 HTTP calls.
14. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L199–205.** On a miss it scans every key of `IMAGE_CACHE` with a prefix test. This costs O(cache size) per miss. It is small now, but the cache grows without limit.
15. **`get_car_image`, L560–573, together with `get_wikipedia_image` L66–71, L162, L195.** The cache key is computed twice, the cache is checked twice and the result is stored twice for the same request.
16. **`query_vespa` L219–225 and `query_vespa_facets` L313–319.** Both build the same `features` list, and `chat` (L500–502) and `update_preferences` (L534–537) always call both with the same `preferences`. The `'{' + ','.join(features) + '}'` string is therefore built twice per request.
17. **`query_vespa` L276 and `query_vespa_facets` L371.** Both send `"trace.level": 1`, so Vespa produces trace data and the app sends it on to the browser, where nothing reads it.
18. **`query_vespa` L279 and `query_vespa_facets` L387.** `json.dumps(query, indent=2)` pretty-prints the whole query only for a log line, and `requests.post(json=query)` then serializes it again.
19. **`query_vespa` L283–287 and `query_vespa_facets` L391–395.** Both use `requests.post` with an mTLS client certificate and no shared `Session`. Every request, two per user action, pays a full client-certificate TLS handshake.
20. **`chat`, L472–475.** `session.get('preferences', {}).copy()` is copied again at L475, and the first copy is never used for anything else.
21. **`chat`, L432 and L447–449.** The whole `session['messages']` history is sent to OpenAI on every turn and kept in Flask's cookie session, which is serialized and signed on every response. The cost per turn grows with conversation length, so the total over a conversation grows quadratically. This is a design-level lead. L445 also prints the full system prompt on every filtered request.

## examples/book-search/frontend/app.py
All of this is Streamlit top-level code that needs network access to Vespa.

22. **`<module>`, L16.** Streamlit reruns the whole script on every widget interaction, so `Vespa(...)` is rebuilt each time. `st.cache_resource` would keep one instance.
23. **`<module>`, L38–41.** The `totalCount` check query (`hits=0`) makes a network round trip on every rerun, meaning every keystroke, slider move and button press, and again after each `st.rerun()` at L82 and L86. Its result only matters on the first run, so it could be cached in `st.session_state` or with `st.cache_resource`.
24. **`feed_catalog`, L20–25.** It makes one synchronous `feed_data_point` HTTP request per document. pyvespa's `feed_iterable` would batch these and send them concurrently.

## examples/google-cloud/cloud-functions/python/main.py
All of this depends on network access to GCS.

25. **`get_blobs`, L88.** It builds a new `storage.Client()`, which includes finding credentials, on every invocation. A module-level client would be reused across warm instances.
26. **`listfiles`, L43–47.** It lists every blob in the bucket and filters by substring in Python. `list_blobs(match_glob=...)` would filter on the server, but only if the substring semantics can be written as a glob. That needs checking.
27. **`getlogs`, L58–70.** It downloads every matching `.zst` blob whole (L65), decompresses it fully in memory (L66) and runs `json.loads` on every line before testing `uri_filter`. A cheap substring check on the raw line before parsing would skip most of the parsing. One caveat applies. JSON escapes such as `\/` could make a raw-byte check miss a real match. Separately, if `uri_filter` is None, L69 raises TypeError. That is a bug, not waste.

## examples/aws/lambda/hello_function.py
`hello_handler` (L6–14) does nothing wasteful.

## examples/operations/monitoring/album-recommendation-monitoring/vespa/wait-for-and-launch.py
28. **`<module>`, L21.** It downloads the full response body only to check `status_code`. `stream=True` or a HEAD request would be enough. Retry uses exponential backoff (L16), so there is no busy-wait. Impact is negligible. Needs network.

## examples/part-purchases-demo/ext/parts.py
Pure-ish top-level code that a synthetic CSV can drive.

29. **`<module>`, L19.** `time.strptime` plus `time.mktime` runs on every row. `strptime` is a pure-Python, regex-based parser. `datetime.fromisoformat(...).timestamp()`, which is implemented in C, would be cheaper. Local-time handling around DST transitions would need checking to confirm the output is identical.
30. **`<module>`, L20–21.** `del row['date']` followed by reassignment only moves the key to the end of the dict, and `sort_keys=True` makes that order irrelevant.
31. **`<module>`, L25.** `json.dumps(..., indent=0)` adds newlines, and `.replace('\n','')` makes a second pass over the string to strip them. `json.dumps(part, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ': '))` gives the same bytes in one pass. Escaped `\n` inside values is unaffected either way.

## examples/model-exporting/export_hf_model_from_hf.py
Needs the model download and files.

32. **`export_model`, L43–49.** `tokenizer.save_pretrained` writes every tokenizer file, and the loop then deletes all except `tokenizer.json`. Saving only the backend tokenizer would skip writing them.
33. **`export_model`, L52.** `import onnx` is never used, and importing it is pure overhead.
34. **`main`, L66–76.** With `--patch_tokenizer`, it reads back the `tokenizer.json` it just wrote, parses it, and rewrites it with `json.dumps`, building the whole string before `f.write`. Patching before the first write would avoid one parse and one write.

## examples/model-exporting/export_model_from_hf.py
35. **`export_model`, L42–48.** Same write-then-delete pattern as item 32, keeping `vocab.txt`. Needs the model and files.

## commerce-product-ranking/scripts/evaluate.py
Pandas preprocessing that synthetic parquet and qrels files can drive. The evaluator itself needs network.

36. **`main`, L52–55.** It reads the whole parquet file, all columns, then filters three times, producing three intermediate frames. `read_parquet(columns=[...], filters=[...])` would push both the column selection and the filters down to pyarrow, or the three masks could at least be combined into one.
37. **`main`, L63–65.** A Python lambda with a generator and `.format` runs per group. Building `"id:" + product_id.astype(str)` once and then using `groupby().agg(" ".join)` would be cheaper. Impact is low.
38. **`main`, L75–76.** `grouped_df.set_index("query_id")` is computed twice.
39. **`main`, L91–95.** `groupby.apply` with a Python lambda builds a dict per group. A single pass over `zip(qid, pid, rel)` into a defaultdict avoids the per-group apply overhead.
40. **`main`, L98.** `set(query_dict.keys()) & set(grouped_qrels.keys())` copies both key sets. Dict key views support `&` directly. Impact is negligible.

## commerce-product-ranking/scripts/export-bi-encoder.py and export-cross-encoder.py
41. **`<module>`.** Neither file has material waste. The only extras are unused imports (`AutoModelForSequenceClassification` at bi-encoder L3, `torch.nn` at bi-encoder L8 and cross-encoder L7), and transformers loads torch anyway. Both need the model and network.

## use-case-shopping/convert_meta.py
`process` is pure. `main` reads stdin.

42. **`main`, L57.** `sys.stdin.readlines()` loads the whole input into a list before processing. Iterating `sys.stdin` directly avoids that.
43. **`main`, L54, L64, L67.** Every document is kept in `output_data`, then `json.dumps(indent=2)` builds one huge string. The peak memory is several times the input size, and the indentation inflates the bytes written. Streaming output would fix this, but writing JSONL changes the format. Writing the array element by element would keep it.
44. **`process`, L13.** `int(time.time())` is called once per document. It could be taken once, though that changes the result very slightly.
45. **`process`, L37–40.** `"|".join(category[0:level+1])` re-slices and re-joins each prefix, which is O(L²) per category. Hierarchies are short, so impact is low. `fields["categories_text"] +=` builds a string through a dict item in a loop.
46. **`process`, L44–45.** `data["related"][key]` is looked up again for every key. `.values()` would avoid the repeated lookup.

## use-case-shopping/convert_reviews.py
47. **`main`, L46 and L58.** Same `readlines` and whole-list `json.dumps(indent=2)` pattern as items 42 and 43.
48. **`process`, L20–34.** It builds `fields` before checking `contains_illegal_chars`, so rejected records were built for nothing. This is trivial. Pure.

## use-case-shopping/create_suggestions.py
All top-level code. Needs the spaCy model and the input file. `filter`, `filter_content` and `clean_text` are pure.

49. **`<module>`, L10.** `spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")` loads the full pipeline, including `ner` and `lemmatizer`. Only `doc.noun_chunks` is used, which needs the parser and POS tags. Excluding the `ner` and `lemmatizer` components would cut work on every document.
50. **`<module>`, L102.** `nlp(content)` runs once per document. `nlp.pipe(titles, batch_size=...)` batches the work and is substantially faster.
51. **`<module>`, L79–80 and L97–98.** The same JSON file is opened and parsed twice.
52. **`<module>`, L112–118.** For every noun phrase it scans `vocab.keys()` linearly with a substring test until one hits. That is O(|vocab| × len) per phrase, and probably the largest cost after spaCy. Phrases are at most 64 characters, so testing each substring of the phrase against a set gives the same answer. Also, `re.split` at L90 yields `''` whenever a title ends in punctuation. If `''` is in `vocab`, the test is always True and the loop only wastes time reaching it. I have not checked whether `''` actually occurs in the data.
53. **`<module>`, L88–95.** It counts occurrences into `vocab`, but only the keys are ever used. A set would do.
54. **`filter`, L57–65.** It runs 33 separate substring scans per text and is called for every title and every noun chunk. One compiled alternation regex would do the same in a single pass. L60 is dead code, because `len(text) < 3` already returned at L58.
55. **`filter_content`, L67–71.** It loops in Python, where `text.startswith(tuple(invalid_starts))` does the same in a single C call.
56. **`<module>`, L84.** `re.split` splits the whole title and then slices `[0:4]`. `maxsplit=4` would stop early with the same first four elements. L84, L90 and L124 pass the pattern string each call, which costs a regex-cache lookup each time. Impact is low.
57. **`<module>`, L121 and L5/L8.** `suggest = []` is never used, and `json` is imported twice. Impact is negligible.

## incremental-search/search-as-you-type/feed_to_vespa.py
Depends on the network and `curl`. `find`, `get_document_id` and `get_feed_docids` are pure-ish.

58. **`call` L22–25, `vespa_post` L48–58, `vespa_delete` L37–45.** It spawns one `curl` process per document for feeding and per document for deletion. Each spawn costs a fork/exec plus a new TCP/TLS connection. A `requests.Session` or `vespa feed` would reuse connections.
59. **`update_endpoint`, L139–141 and L155–160.** When both `do_index_removal_before_feed` and `do_feed` are set, L141 deletes every indexed document. L155 then computes `docids_to_remove` from the stale `docids_in_index` and deletes those documents again, one curl process per id.
60. **`update_endpoint` L149 → `get_feed_docids` L110–111, and L167 → `vespa_feed` → `get_docs` L89–91.** Each feed file is opened and parsed twice. `get_docs` also never closes its file.
61. **`update_endpoint`, L149.** `docids_in_feed = docids_in_feed.union(...)` allocates a new set on every iteration. `update()` would grow the set in place. L112 builds a list only to turn it into a set. Impact is low.

## incremental-search/search-suggestions/accepted_words.py
Pure-ish given a file.

62. **`read_common_words`, L17–19.** It reads the whole file with `readlines()` and then adds lines one by one. A set comprehension over the file object does the same in one pass.
63. **`process_docs`, L29–32.** Terms are added one at a time in a Python loop. `term_set.update(clean_text(...))` does it in C.
64. **`write_to_file`, L41–42.** One `f.write(term + "\n")` per term, with a string concatenation each time. `f.write("\n".join(...))` or `writelines` would replace the per-term calls. Impact is low.

## incremental-search/search-suggestions/count_terms.py
Pure apart from file I/O. A good candidate for testing locally with synthetic docs.

65. **`process_docs`, L100–103.** For each distinct term it scans all `doc_counts` to compute `docs`. That is O(T × D). Each per-document dict has unique keys, so adding 1 per term inside the L91–97 loop gives the same result in one pass, and `doc_counts` (L85–87) would no longer have to be kept in memory. This is the largest lead in this file.
66. **`process_docs`, L92.** `total_count = sum([...])` is computed for every document and never used.
67. **`process_doc`, L76–79.** `list(title_counts.keys()) + list(content_counts.keys())` builds two lists. Terms present in both are computed twice. `title_counts.keys() | content_counts.keys()` or `Counter` addition avoids both.
68. **`count_terms`, L59–62.** It calls a lambda per word through `any(map(...))` and slices `doc[i:i+win_len]` twice. For `term_length > 1` it re-checks words already known to be common. Precomputing an `is_common` array, or the index of the last common word, once per document would remove the repeated checks.
69. **`write_json_file`, L27 and L39.** `re.sub(r" ", "/", term)` replaces a single literal character, and `str.replace` is cheaper. `json.dump(indent=2)` inflates the output, and changing that changes the format.
70. **`read_common_words`, L45–47.** Same `readlines` pattern as item 62.

## Where to start
These look like the leads with the largest likely savings:
- item 65, the O(T × D) loop in `count_terms.py::process_docs`
- items 49–52, spaCy batching and component pruning plus the vocab scan in `create_suggestions.py`
- items 4 and 8, `iterrows` in `preprocess.py`, and the full-dataset work in sample mode (items 2, 3, 7)
- items 58–60, one curl process per document, deleting twice, and parsing each feed file twice in `feed_to_vespa.py`
- items 13, 19 and 23, failures that are not cached, no connection reuse, and the check query on every rerun in the two webapps

Items 28, 33, 40, 41 and 57 are negligible.

This file depends on network calls to OpenAI, Vespa and Wikipedia. `load_system_prompt` and the query-building parts of `query_vespa` and `query_vespa_facets` are pure-ish.

9. **`load_system_prompt`, L46–49, called from `chat` at L435.** `system_prompt.txt` is opened and read from disk on every `/api/chat` request. It could be read once when the module loads.
10. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L86, 96, 118, 146, 179.** Every call is a bare `requests.get` with no shared `Session`, so each one opens a new TCP and TLS connection to en.wikipedia.org. A single lookup can make three or more of these calls.
11. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L133–163.** It makes one sequential `imageinfo` HTTP request per matching image. The MediaWiki API accepts several titles joined with `|`, so one request could cover all of them.
12. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L167–196.** The fallback loop asks again for the same images the first loop already queried, whenever they match a keyword but returned no URL and are not .svg/.png/.gif. It also recomputes `image.get("title","").lower()`.
13. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L103, 127, 208 (failures are not cached).** When no image is found it returns `None` without writing to `IMAGE_CACHE`. Every later request for that make and model repeats the whole Wikipedia sequence, two to N+3 HTTP calls.
14. **`get_wikipedia_image`, L199–205.** On a miss it scans every key of `IMAGE_CACHE` with a prefix test. This costs O(cache size) per miss. It is small now, but the cache grows without limit.
15. **`get_car_image`, L560–573, together with `get_wikipedia_image` L66–71, L162, L195.** The cache key is computed twice, the cache is checked twice and the result is stored twice for the same request.
16. **`query_vespa` L219–225 and `query_vespa_facets` L313–319.** Both build the same `features` list, and `chat` (L500–502) and `update_preferences` (L534–537) always call both with the same `preferences`. The `'{' + ','.join(features) + '}'` string is therefore built twice per request.
17. **`query_vespa` L276 and `query_vespa_facets` L371.** Both send `"trace.level": 1`, so Vespa produces trace data and the app sends it on to the browser, where nothing reads it.
18. **`query_vespa` L279 and `query_vespa_facets` L387.** `json.dumps(query, indent=2)` pretty-prints the whole query only for a log line, and `requests.post(json=query)` then serializes it again.
19. **`query_vespa` L283–287 and `query_vespa_facets` L391–395.** Both use `requests.post` with an mTLS client certificate and no shared `Session`. Every request, two per user action, pays a full client-certificate TLS handshake.
20. **`chat`, L472–475.** `session.get('preferences', {}).copy()` is copied again at L475, and the first copy is never used for anything else.
21. **`chat`, L432 and L447–449.** The whole `session['messages']` history is sent to OpenAI on every turn and kept in Flask's cookie session, which is serialized and signed on every response. The cost per turn grows with conversation length, so the total over a conversation grows quadratically. This is a design-level lead. L445 also prints the full system prompt on every filtered request.

## examples/book-search/frontend/app.py
All of this is Streamlit top-level code that needs network access to Vespa.

22. **`<module>`, L16.** Streamlit reruns the whole script on every widget interaction, so `Vespa(...)` is rebuilt each time. `st.cache_resource` would keep one instance.
23. **`<module>`, L38–41.** The `totalCount` check query (`hits=0`) makes a network round trip on every rerun, meaning every keystroke, slider move and button press, and again after each `st.rerun()` at L82 and L86. Its result only matters on the first run, so it could be cached in `st.session_state` or with `st.cache_resource`.
24. **`feed_catalog`, L20–25.** It makes one synchronous `feed_data_point` HTTP request per document. pyvespa's `feed_iterable` would batch these and send them concurrently.

## examples/google-cloud/cloud-functions/python/main.py
All of this depends on network access to GCS.

25. **`get_blobs`, L88.** It builds a new `storage.Client()`, which includes finding credentials, on every invocation. A module-level client would be reused across warm instances.
26. **`listfiles`, L43–47.** It lists every blob in the bucket and filters by substring in Python. `list_blobs(match_glob=...)` would filter on the server, but only if the substring semantics can be written as a glob. That needs checking.
27. **`getlogs`, L58–70.** It downloads every matching `.zst` blob whole (L65), decompresses it fully in memory (L66) and runs `json.loads` on every line before testing `uri_filter`. A cheap substring check on the raw line before parsing would skip most of the parsing. One caveat applies. JSON escapes such as `\/` could make a raw-byte check miss a real match. Separately, if `uri_filter` is None, L69 raises TypeError. That is a bug, not waste.

## examples/aws/lambda/hello_function.py
`hello_handler` (L6–14) does nothing wasteful.

## examples/operations/monitoring/album-recommendation-monitoring/vespa/wait-for-and-launch.py
28. **`<module>`, L21.** It downloads the full response body only to check `status_code`. `stream=True` or a HEAD request would be enough. Retry uses exponential backoff (L16), so there is no busy-wait. Impact is negligible. Needs network.

## examples/part-purchases-demo/ext/parts.py
Pure-ish top-level code that a synthetic CSV can drive.

29. **`<module>`, L19.** `time.strptime` plus `time.mktime` runs on every row. `strptime` is a pure-Python, regex-based parser. `datetime.fromisoformat(...).timestamp()`, which is implemented in C, would be cheaper. Local-time handling around DST transitions would need checking to confirm the output is identical.
30. **`<module>`, L20–21.** `del row['date']` followed by reassignment only moves the key to the end of the dict, and `sort_keys=True` makes that order irrelevant.
31. **`<module>`, L25.** `json.dumps(..., indent=0)` adds newlines, and `.replace('\n','')` makes a second pass over the string to strip them. `json.dumps(part, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ': '))` gives the same bytes in one pass. Escaped `\n` inside values is unaffected either way.

## examples/model-exporting/export_hf_model_from_hf.py
Needs the model download and files.

32. **`export_model`, L43–49.** `tokenizer.save_pretrained` writes every tokenizer file, and the loop then deletes all except `tokenizer.json`. Saving only the backend tokenizer would skip writing them.
33. **`export_model`, L52.** `import onnx` is never used, and importing it is pure overhead.
34. **`main`, L66–76.** With `--patch_tokenizer`, it reads back the `tokenizer.json` it just wrote, parses it, and rewrites it with `json.dumps`, building the whole string before `f.write`. Patching before the first write would avoid one parse and one write.

## examples/model-exporting/export_model_from_hf.py
35. **`export_model`, L42–48.** Same write-then-delete pattern as item 32, keeping `vocab.txt`. Needs the model and files.

## commerce-product-ranking/scripts/evaluate.py
Pandas preprocessing that synthetic parquet and qrels files can drive. The evaluator itself needs network.

36. **`main`, L52–55.** It reads the whole parquet file, all columns, then filters three times, producing three intermediate frames. `read_parquet(columns=[...], filters=[...])` would push both the column selection and the filters down to pyarrow, or the three masks could at least be combined into one.
37. **`main`, L63–65.** A Python lambda with a generator and `.format` runs per group. Building `"id:" + product_id.astype(str)` once and then using `groupby().agg(" ".join)` would be cheaper. Impact is low.
38. **`main`, L75–76.** `grouped_df.set_index("query_id")` is computed twice.
39. **`main`, L91–95.** `groupby.apply` with a Python lambda builds a dict per group. A single pass over `zip(qid, pid, rel)` into a defaultdict avoids the per-group apply overhead.
40. **`main`, L98.** `set(query_dict.keys()) & set(grouped_qrels.keys())` copies both key sets. Dict key views support `&` directly. Impact is negligible.

## commerce-product-ranking/scripts/export-bi-encoder.py and export-cross-encoder.py
41. **`<module>`.** Neither file has material waste. The only extras are unused imports (`AutoModelForSequenceClassification` at bi-encoder L3, `torch.nn` at bi-encoder L8 and cross-encoder L7), and transformers loads torch anyway. Both need the model and network.

## use-case-shopping/convert_meta.py
`process` is pure. `main` reads stdin.

42. **`main`, L57.** `sys.stdin.readlines()` loads the whole input into a list before processing. Iterating `sys.stdin` directly avoids that.
43. **`main`, L54, L64, L67.** Every document is kept in `output_data`, then `json.dumps(indent=2)` builds one huge string. The peak memory is several times the input size, and the indentation inflates the bytes written. Streaming output would fix this, but writing JSONL changes the format. Writing the array element by element would keep it.
44. **`process`, L13.** `int(time.time())` is called once per document. It could be taken once, though that changes the result very slightly.
45. **`process`, L37–40.** `"|".join(category[0:level+1])` re-slices and re-joins each prefix, which is O(L²) per category. Hierarchies are short, so impact is low. `fields["categories_text"] +=` builds a string through a dict item in a loop.
46. **`process`, L44–45.** `data["related"][key]` is looked up again for every key. `.values()` would avoid the repeated lookup.

## use-case-shopping/convert_reviews.py
47. **`main`, L46 and L58.** Same `readlines` and whole-list `json.dumps(indent=2)` pattern as items 42 and 43.
48. **`process`, L20–34.** It builds `fields` before checking `contains_illegal_chars`, so rejected records were built for nothing. This is trivial. Pure.

## use-case-shopping/create_suggestions.py
All top-level code. Needs the spaCy model and the input file. `filter`, `filter_content` and `clean_text` are pure.

49. **`<module>`, L10.** `spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")` loads the full pipeline, including `ner` and `lemmatizer`. Only `doc.noun_chunks` is used, which needs the parser and POS tags. Excluding the `ner` and `lemmatizer` components would cut work on every document.
50. **`<module>`, L102.** `nlp(content)` runs once per document. `nlp.pipe(titles, batch_size=...)` batches the work and is substantially faster.
51. **`<module>`, L79–80 and L97–98.** The same JSON file is opened and parsed twice.
52. **`<module>`, L112–118.** For every noun phrase it scans `vocab.keys()` linearly with a substring test until one hits. That is O(|vocab| × len) per phrase, and probably the largest cost after spaCy. Phrases are at most 64 characters, so testing each substring of the phrase against a set gives the same answer. Also, `re.split` at L90 yields `''` whenever a title ends in punctuation. If `''` is in `vocab`, the test is always True and the loop only wastes time reaching it. I have not checked whether `''` actually occurs in the data.
53. **`<module>`, L88–95.** It counts occurrences into `vocab`, but only the keys are ever used. A set would do.
54. **`filter`, L57–65.** It runs 33 separate substring scans per text and is called for every title and every noun chunk. One compiled alternation regex would do the same in a single pass. L60 is dead code, because `len(text) < 3` already returned at L58.
55. **`filter_content`, L67–71.** It loops in Python, where `text.startswith(tuple(invalid_starts))` does the same in a single C call.
56. **`<module>`, L84.** `re.split` splits the whole title and then slices `[0:4]`. `maxsplit=4` would stop early with the same first four elements. L84, L90 and L124 pass the pattern string each call, which costs a regex-cache lookup each time. Impact is low.
57. **`<module>`, L121 and L5/L8.** `suggest = []` is never used, and `json` is imported twice. Impact is negligible.

## incremental-search/search-as-you-type/feed_to_vespa.py
Depends on the network and `curl`. `find`, `get_document_id` and `get_feed_docids` are pure-ish.

58. **`call` L22–25, `vespa_post` L48–58, `vespa_delete` L37–45.** It spawns one `curl` process per document for feeding and per document for deletion. Each spawn costs a fork/exec plus a new TCP/TLS connection. A `requests.Session` or `vespa feed` would reuse connections.
59. **`update_endpoint`, L139–141 and L155–160.** When both `do_index_removal_before_feed` and `do_feed` are set, L141 deletes every indexed document. L155 then computes `docids_to_remove` from the stale `docids_in_index` and deletes those documents again, one curl process per id.
60. **`update_endpoint` L149 → `get_feed_docids` L110–111, and L167 → `vespa_feed` → `get_docs` L89–91.** Each feed file is opened and parsed twice. `get_docs` also never closes its file.
61. **`update_endpoint`, L149.** `docids_in_feed = docids_in_feed.union(...)` allocates a new set on every iteration. `update()` would grow the set in place. L112 builds a list only to turn it into a set. Impact is low.

## incremental-search/search-suggestions/accepted_words.py
Pure-ish given a file.

62. **`read_common_words`, L17–19.** It reads the whole file with `readlines()` and then adds lines one by one. A set comprehension over the file object does the same in one pass.
63. **`process_docs`, L29–32.** Terms are added one at a time in a Python loop. `term_set.update(clean_text(...))` does it in C.
64. **`write_to_file`, L41–42.** One `f.write(term + "\n")` per term, with a string concatenation each time. `f.write("\n".join(...))` or `writelines` would replace the per-term calls. Impact is low.

## incremental-search/search-suggestions/count_terms.py
Pure apart from file I/O. A good candidate for testing locally with synthetic docs.

65. **`process_docs`, L100–103.** For each distinct term it scans all `doc_counts` to compute `docs`. That is O(T × D). Each per-document dict has unique keys, so adding 1 per term inside the L91–97 loop gives the same result in one pass, and `doc_counts` (L85–87) would no longer have to be kept in memory. This is the largest lead in this file.
66. **`process_docs`, L92.** `total_count = sum([...])` is computed for every document and never used.
67. **`process_doc`, L76–79.** `list(title_counts.keys()) + list(content_counts.keys())` builds two lists. Terms present in both are computed twice. `title_counts.keys() | content_counts.keys()` or `Counter` addition avoids both.
68. **`count_terms`, L59–62.** It calls a lambda per word through `any(map(...))` and slices `doc[i:i+win_len]` twice. For `term_length > 1` it re-checks words already known to be common. Precomputing an `is_common` array, or the index of the last common word, once per document would remove the repeated checks.
69. **`write_json_file`, L27 and L39.** `re.sub(r" ", "/", term)` replaces a single literal character, and `str.replace` is cheaper. `json.dump(indent=2)` inflates the output, and changing that changes the format.
70. **`read_common_words`, L45–47.** Same `readlines` pattern as item 62.

## Where to start
These look like the leads with the largest likely savings:
- item 65, the O(T × D) loop in `count_terms.py::process_docs`
- items 49–52, spaCy batching and component pruning plus the vocab scan in `create_suggestions.py`
- items 4 and 8, `iterrows` in `preprocess.py`, and the full-dataset work in sample mode (items 2, 3, 7)
- items 58–60, one curl process per document, deleting twice, and parsing each feed file twice in `feed_to_vespa.py`
- items 13, 19 and 23, failures that are not cached, no connection reuse, and the check query on every rerun in the two webapps

Items 28, 33, 40, 41 and 57 are negligible.

    # Only use queries that have associated qrels
    common_query_ids = set(query_dict.keys()) & set(grouped_qrels.keys())
    if not common_query_ids:

2. **`perform_cross_validation`, L268–275.** The model goes through `dump_model()` → `json.dumps` → one `re.sub` over the whole JSON string per feature (`feature_name_mapping`) → `json.loads` → `json.dump` (L280). Editing `model_json["feature_names"]` and `feature_infos` directly, or one alternation regex followed by writing the string as is, would do the same job. Pure-ish given a trained booster.
3. **`perform_cross_validation`, L249–254.** A nested loop scans all of `feature_name_mapping` for each name in `final_features`, which is O(F²). An inverted dict would do. Pure.
4. **`perform_cross_validation`, L99–104.** `col in feature_cols` is a list membership test inside a loop over `df.columns`, O(F²). `stripped_feature_mapping.get(col, col)` would do. Pure.
5. **`perform_cross_validation`, L111 and L120.** `c in feature_cols` is again a list membership test, and `feature_cols.index(c)` is a linear scan per categorical column. Pure.
6. **`perform_cross_validation`, L165–177.** The `params` dict is rebuilt identically every fold. It is loop-invariant; the cost is tiny.
7. **`perform_cross_validation`, L196–199.** `oof_pred[val_idx]` is fancy-indexed twice after assignment, and each read makes a copy. Keeping the `model.predict` result in a local avoids both copies.
8. **`perform_cross_validation`, L78.** `df[c].nunique(dropna=False)` runs once per column in Python. One vectorized `df.nunique(dropna=False)` would do. Pure.
9. **`strip_feature_prefix`, L25.** `re.sub` takes a pattern string on every call, so each call pays a lookup in the `re` cache. A precompiled pattern or `str.removeprefix` would do. It is called F times, so the cost is minor. Pure.
10. **`save_feature_importance`, L44.** `iterrows` over 10 rows is trivial, but zipping the two columns would do. Pure.

## rag-blueprint/eval/train_logistic_regression.py

11. **`perform_cross_validation`, L102–106.** `X[feature].describe()` runs once per feature and computes count, quartiles (a sort or partition) and the rest, but only mean, std, min and max are printed. One `X.agg(["mean","std","min","max"])` would do. Pure given a DataFrame.
12. **`perform_cross_validation`, L138–139.** `model.predict` and `model.predict_proba` each compute the decision function. `y_pred = (y_pred_proba > 0.5)` is equivalent except at exact ties. Pure.
13. **`perform_cross_validation`, L192–195, and `save_coefficients_expression`, L36–39.** `transformed_coefs` and `transformed_intercept` are computed twice, the same way. Pure.

## rag-blueprint/eval/collect_pyvespa.py

28. **`<module>`, L15.** `subgraph = subgraph_builder.compile()` runs on every rerun and the result is never used. `subgraph.py` L254 already compiles it once at import.

## langgraph_modules/subgraph.py

## langgraph_modules/main_graph.py

37. **`VespaRetrieverTool`, L41.** `thread_config` is built with no checkpointer attached. Trivial.
38. **`<module>`, L51–56.** Runs once per process because the module is cached on import. No waste.
39. **`assistant`, L67.** `[sys_msg] + state["messages"]` builds a list on every call. Inherent to the pattern and minor.

## vespa_module/vespa_retriever.py

40. **`VespaRetriever`, L67.** A new `Vespa` client is constructed for every retrieval. Needs the network.
41. **`VespaRetriever`, L94–96.** `str(q)` serializes the query for the `print`, then `query(yql=q)` serializes it again. L60 and L106 print debug output.

## vespa_module/update_vespa.py

44. **`<module>`, L67–95.** An endless poll every 3 s. It is intended as a simulator, but it runs forever.
45. **`fetch_documents`, L27.** Opens a new `syncio` session (new connection and mTLS handshake) on every iteration.
46. **`update_document_quantity`, L42.** pyvespa 1.2.9's `Vespa.update_data` opens a fresh `VespaSync(pool_connections=1)` on every call (application.py L1481), so each document update makes a new connection. One session per batch would do. L51 prints `response.json` for every update.
47. **`<module>`, L3–11.** `requests`, `sys`, `os` and `VespaResponse` are imported but unused. `streamlit` is imported only to read secrets, which costs import time.

## utils/helpers.py, utils/secrets.py, models/state.py

48. **`get_latest_ai_or_human_message`, L5–6.** The string comparisons on `messagetype` are loop-invariant and repeated per message. Resolving the target class once would do. Trivial. Pure.

## examples/in-context-learning/categorize_group.py

49. **`inference`, L128–209.** Each call builds 12 request dicts and uses one (`query_request_bm25_no_group_10`, L210). That is 11 unneeded dicts per query, for up to 1000 queries. Pure up to the HTTP call.
50. **`inference`, L211.** A bare `requests.post` per query has no `Session`, so there is no connection keep-alive across the 1000 queries. The `select *` with `summary()` also returns every field, but only `text` and `label` are read (L84–85).
51. **`get_label`, L66 and L68.** `result not in label_names` is a list membership test over 77 labels, done twice per call. A set would do. Pure apart from the LLM call.
52. **`get_label`, L41–52.** The prompt includes `Text: {text}, Category:` twice, which duplicates tokens sent to the LLM. L38's `examples.reverse()` mutates the caller's list in place; that is a side effect, not a waste.
53. **`<module>`, L231 and L273.** Loads the full test split (3,080 rows per the published dataset card, not checked here) but breaks at 1000. `split="test[:1000]"` would load only what is used.
54. **`timer_decorator`, L7.** Unused. No runtime cost.

## examples/in-context-learning/feed_examples.py

55. **`<module>`, L14–25.** One `print(json.dumps(...))` per row. The rest is inherent. A cumulative `hash_object` with `hexdigest()` per row is O(1) per row, so it is not a waste. Needs the dataset.

## examples/mcp-server-app/script/generate_data.py

56. **`generate_job`, L73, and `generate_candidate`, L104.** `list(skills.keys())` builds a list per call although the sampled list is already available. `generate_job` L87 calls `datetime.now()` per job when it could be computed once. Pure.
57. **`save_vespa_feed`, L124–130.** Builds the full `output` list and one joined string in memory before writing. The key `f'{doc_type}_id'` is rebuilt per item although it is invariant. Small at 105 documents. Pure apart from the file write.

## embedder-auto-training-evaluation/data-preparation

58. **`add-title-if-missing.py::<module>` L4–8, `convert-for-feeding.py::<module>` L7–19, `prepend-passage.py::<module>` L4–11.** One `print` per line is the only overhead. The JSON parse and dump are inherent. Pure stdin-to-stdout scripts, easy to benchmark.

## embedder-auto-training-evaluation/training-evaluation/evaluate.py

59. **`search`, L22–25.** The bare `except:` retry repeats a request that the mounted `Retry(total=20, connect=20, backoff_factor=0.3)` adapter has already retried up to 20 times with backoff. A failing query is therefore attempted about twice as often. The same pattern appears in `positives-negatives.py::search` L22–25.

    Smaller items:
    - `evaluate.py::search` L11–21: the invariant parts of the `query_request` dict are rebuilt per query.
    - `evaluate.py::search` L35: `str(query_id)` is recomputed for each of up to 100 hits.
    - `evaluate.py::main` L85: `progress.write` prints every query.
    - `evaluate.py::main` L88–89: pandas is imported and used only to write a space-separated file from the list of dicts.

    Needs the network.

## positives-negatives.py

`search` L11–21: the invariant request dict is rebuilt per query, and it has the same duplicate retry as #59. The membership test at L41 is fine, because `positive_documents` is a `dict_keys` view with O(1) lookup. `--query_field` is parsed but never used.

## train.py

60. **`TrainDataset.__init__`, L11–20.** `file.readlines()` materializes each whole file before iterating. Every document in the corpus is kept with all its fields, but `__getitem__` only reads `["text"]`, and only for IDs referenced by queries. Filtering to the referenced IDs would cut memory and parsing. Needs files; easy to run with synthetic JSONL.

    Smaller items:
    - `TrainDataset.__getitem__` L27–33: `list.pop(0)` plus `append` rotates the positives and negatives lists in O(n) per item. An index counter or `deque.rotate` would be O(1).
    - `main` L69–74: `checkpoint_save_steps=len(train_dataloader)` writes a full model checkpoint every epoch into the same directory that `model.save` then writes the final model to. That is extra disk I/O if only the final model is used. Training itself needs a GPU.

The biggest measurable CPU leads are #1 (per-round train-set AUC), #2 (JSON round trip with per-feature regex), #11 (describe per feature) and #12 (double prediction). All four can be benchmarked locally on synthetic data. The rest are mostly loop-invariant rebuilds of small objects or connection and LLM-token costs that need network access to measure.

52. **`get_label`, L41–52.** The prompt includes `Text: {text}, Category:` twice, which duplicates tokens sent to the LLM. L38's `examples.reverse()` mutates the caller's list in place; that is a side effect, not a waste.
53. **`<module>`, L231 and L273.** Loads the full test split (3,080 rows per the published dataset card, not checked here) but breaks at 1000. `split="test[:1000]"` would load only what is used.
54. **`timer_decorator`, L7.** Unused. No runtime cost.

## examples/in-context-learning/feed_examples.py

55. **`<module>`, L14–25.** One `print(json.dumps(...))` per row. The rest is inherent. A cumulative `hash_object` with `hexdigest()` per row is O(1) per row, so it is not a waste. Needs the dataset.

## examples/mcp-server-app/script/generate_data.py

56. **`generate_job`, L73, and `generate_candidate`, L104.** `list(skills.keys())` builds a list per call although the sampled list is already available. `generate_job` L87 calls `datetime.now()` per job when it could be computed once. Pure.
57. **`save_vespa_feed`, L124–130.** Builds the full `output` list and one joined string in memory before writing. The key `f'{doc_type}_id'` is rebuilt per item although it is invariant. Small at 105 documents. Pure apart from the file write.

## embedder-auto-training-evaluation/data-preparation

58. **`add-title-if-missing.py::<module>` L4–8, `convert-for-feeding.py::<module>` L7–19, `prepend-passage.py::<module>` L4–11.** One `print` per line is the only overhead. The JSON parse and dump are inherent. Pure stdin-to-stdout scripts, easy to benchmark.

## embedder-auto-training-evaluation/training-evaluation/evaluate.py

59. **`search`, L22–25.** The bare `except:` retry repeats a request that the mounted `Retry(total=20, connect=20, backoff_factor=0.3)` adapter has already retried up to 20 times with backoff. A failing query is therefore attempted about twice as often. The same pattern appears in `positives-negatives.py::search` L22–25.

    Smaller items:
    - `evaluate.py::search` L11–21: the invariant parts of the `query_request` dict are rebuilt per query.
    - `evaluate.py::search` L35: `str(query_id)` is recomputed for each of up to 100 hits.
    - `evaluate.py::main` L85: `progress.write` prints every query.
    - `evaluate.py::main` L88–89: pandas is imported and used only to write a space-separated file from the list of dicts.

    Needs the network.

## positives-negatives.py

`search` L11–21: the invariant request dict is rebuilt per query, and it has the same duplicate retry as #59. The membership test at L41 is fine, because `positive_documents` is a `dict_keys` view with O(1) lookup. `--query_field` is parsed but never used.

## train.py

60. **`TrainDataset.__init__`, L11–20.** `file.readlines()` materializes each whole file before iterating. Every document in the corpus is kept with all its fields, but `__getitem__` only reads `["text"]`, and only for IDs referenced by queries. Filtering to the referenced IDs would cut memory and parsing. Needs files; easy to run with synthetic JSONL.

    Smaller items:
    - `TrainDataset.__getitem__` L27–33: `list.pop(0)` plus `append` rotates the positives and negatives lists in O(n) per item. An index counter or `deque.rotate` would be O(1).
    - `main` L69–74: `checkpoint_save_steps=len(train_dataloader)` writes a full model checkpoint every epoch into the same directory that `model.save` then writes the final model to. That is extra disk I/O if only the final model is used. Training itself needs a GPU.

The biggest measurable CPU leads are #1 (per-round train-set AUC), #2 (JSON round trip with per-feature regex), #11 (describe per feature) and #12 (double prediction). All four can be benchmarked locally on synthetic data. The rest are mostly loop-invariant rebuilds of small objects or connection and LLM-token costs that need network access to measure.

content.text: Group 3's report is in, and groups 2 and 5 are still running.

I read all 26 files in full, including module-level script code (2,470 lines in total, counted with `wc -l`). I also checked four library behaviours on the local interpreter (Python 3.10.12):

- `json.dump` passes `_one_shot=False` to `iterencode`, so it never uses the C encoder (`c_make_encoder`). It runs the pure-Python `_make_iterencode` and calls `fp.write` once per chunk. `json.dumps` does use the C encoder.
- `random.sample` copies any `Set` population, `dict_keys` included, into a `tuple` with a DeprecationWarning. On 3.11 and later it raises TypeError instead.
- `requests.adapters.DEFAULT_POOLSIZE` is 10.
- The `"timestamp"` key built in `mind_data.py` is written once (line 101) and never read anywhere in `news/src/python/`.

Each lead ends with a dependency tag. **P** means pure-ish and callable locally with synthetic inputs. **F** means it needs input or output files, which synthetic temp files can stand in for. **N** means network and **M** means model or GPU.

## news/src/python/convert_embeddings_to_vespa_format.py
1. `read_embeddings` L28, with `convert_user_embeddings` L39 and `convert_news_embeddings` L53. Each vector is parsed into a float32 ndarray, then iterated one numpy scalar at a time for `"%.6f"` formatting. Calling `embedding.tolist()` first formats Python floats with the same output and avoids per-element numpy scalar boxing. [P for the formatting, F for the reader]
2. `convert_user_embeddings` L33 and `convert_news_embeddings` L47. Both load the whole TSV into a dict before writing anything. Streaming line by line would avoid holding every array in memory, but the dict also deduplicates ids (the last one wins), so that behaviour has to be kept. [F]
3. L40-42 and L54-55 build each row with `+` concatenation of three formatted pieces. Trivial. [P]

## news/src/python/convert_to_vespa_format.py
1. `read_impressions_file` L33. `csv.DictReader` builds a 5-key dict for every line, including the long `history` field, but only `impressions` is used. `line.split("\t")` is cheaper. [F]
2. `read_impressions_file` L37-39. `click_map[news_id]` is hashed twice per impression. Trivial. [P]
3. `convert_file` L71. `json.dump(doc, output)` uses the pure-Python encoder and makes several `write` calls per document. `output.write(json.dumps(doc))` uses the C encoder. [F]
4. `convert_file` L53. A `DictReader` dict is built per news line for 6 of its 8 fields. Minor. [F]
5. `generate_random_date` L74-76 calls `fromtimestamp`, `strftime` and `int` for every document. The roughly two-week range could map through a precomputed day table, but the `randint` call has to stay to keep the RNG stream unchanged. [P]

## news/src/python/create_bert_embeddings.py
1. `create_embeddings` L47-48. The tokenizer and the BERT model are loaded inside the function, and `main` L77-78 calls it twice, so both are loaded from disk twice. Hoist them out. [M]
2. `create_embeddings` L30-31 and L41-42. The `categories` and `subcategories` dicts are filled and never read. The `docids` set also duplicates the keys of `titles`. [F]
3. `create_embeddings` L57-58. There is one forward pass per document, with batch size 1 and no `torch.no_grad()`/`inference_mode`, so an autograd graph is recorded for every document. Batching and inference mode would both cut work. [M]
4. `create_embeddings` L59. `outputs[0].tolist()[0][0]` converts the whole `[1, seq≤100, 512]` hidden-state tensor into nested Python lists to read one 512-float CLS vector. Use `outputs[0][0, 0].tolist()`. BertModel also computes a pooler output that is never used. [M]
5. `create_embeddings` L57. `padding=True` on a single pair does nothing. Trivial.
6. `create_embeddings` L63. `len(docids)//100` is computed twice per iteration. Trivial. The same line also raises ZeroDivisionError when there are fewer than 100 documents.
7. `write_embedding` L68-73 makes one `f.write` per float plus one per comma, about 1,024 calls per document. `f.write(",".join(...))` does the same in one call. [P, works with `io.StringIO`]

## news/src/python/create_category_ctrs.py
1. `read_impressions_file` L32 builds a DictReader dict per line. L36-37 test `news_id in news_map` and then index it, and L38-40 index `click_map[category]` twice. [F]
2. `read_content_file` L51. A DictReader dict of 8 fields is built per line to read 2 of them. [F]
3. `write_news_category_ctr_update` L79. `'"category_ctr_ref": {"assign": "%s"}, ' % global_ctr_document_id` does not change between iterations but is formatted once per news row. Trivial. [F, writes to a global path]

## news/src/python/evaluate.py
1. `read_impressions_file` L32-47 with `calc_metrics` L84-86. The whole behaviors.tsv is parsed (split, `int()` on every label, a dict per line), then `random.sample` keeps `sample_size` (default 1000). `random.sample` depends only on `len`, so sampling raw lines first and parsing only the sample gives the same indices. [F]
2. `find_hit` L55-59 called from `predictions` L62-68. Each `news_id` triggers a linear scan of `hits["root"]["children"]`, which is O(n²) per impression. Build `{news_id: relevance}` once per result. [P]
3. `calc_impression` L73. `query_user_embedding` makes an HTTP request for every impression. The same users recur across impressions and across the train and dev passes (L103-104), so a per-`user_id` cache would remove repeat requests. [N]
4. `calc_metrics` L94-99. Four metric calls each sort every impression again (see metrics.py). [P]

## news/src/python/metrics.py (all P)
1. `group_auc` L9-14 calls sklearn `roc_auc_score` once per impression. Its per-call input validation likely dominates on short lists, but I have not measured that.
2. `ndcg_score` L27-30 and `dcg_score` L18-24. The ideal DCG is recomputed with a full `argsort` of `y_true` on every call. `ndcg` is called separately for k=5 and k=10, and `mrr_score` L44 sorts `y_score` again. Per impression that is 3 identical argsorts of `y_score` and 2 of `y_true`.
3. `dcg_score` L20 does a full argsort to take the top k. `argpartition` would do, though the lists are short.
4. `dcg_score` L19 and L21. `np.shape` and `np.take` convert Python-list inputs to arrays (evaluate.py passes lists), and the discounts at L23 are recomputed on every call.

## news/src/python/mind_data.py
1. `MindData.read_data` L93. `datetime.strptime` runs on every impression line and its result goes into `"timestamp"` (L101), which nothing reads. This is unneeded work. L91 `impression_id` is unused too, which is trivial. [F]
2. `MindData.read_news` L63-73 with `MindData.add_entities` L76-80. All unique WikidataIds from title and abstract are collected with a list membership test (`entity_id not in entity_ids`), which is O(n²). Only the first 2 are kept (L73), so collection could stop after 2. [P for `add_entities`]
3. `MindData.lookup_index` L131-134 does an `in` test followed by `[]`. Trivial. [P]
4. `MindData.sample_training_data` L136-157, `add_impressions` L181-201 and `find_clicked` L203-211 run once per epoch (100 epochs in train_mf, 15 in train_cold_start).
   - `find_clicked` repartitions every impression each epoch, although the result never changes between epochs.
   - Each positive and each sampled negative does 3 dict lookups into `self.news_content` (L189-191, L198-200) for a mapping that never changes.
   - Only the negative sampling actually varies by epoch.
   - L145 draws `random.random() <= prob` even when `prob=1.0`. Removing that draw changes the RNG stream, and therefore the sampled negatives. [P with a synthetic instance]
5. `MindData.sample_valid_data` L159-179 is rebuilt on every `eval_model` call. With `prob=1.0` the output is identical each time. L166-169 build three comprehensions and `user_index` before the L170 filter throws away impressions whose labels are all 0 or all 1, and `sum(labels)` is computed twice. [P]
6. `MindData.get_news_content_tensors` L213-229 never changes but is rebuilt every epoch through `save_embeddings` in train_cold_start. [P]
7. train_mf never uses the category, subcategory or entity tensors that `sample_training_data` and `sample_valid_data` build (train_mf L51 and L92 discard them with `_`), so for MF that work is unneeded.

## news/src/python/train_cold_start.py
1. `train_epoch` L99. `total_loss += loss` accumulates the autograd tensor, so each batch adds an `AddBackward` node to a chain that lives until the end of the epoch. Use `loss.item()`. [M]
2. `train_model` L120. `save_embeddings` runs every epoch and overwrites both TSVs, so 14 of 15 writes are discarded (the TODO says "save if better auc"). Saving once after the loop gives the same final files. [M]
3. `train_model` L116 runs a full forward pass over all train impressions every epoch, only to print metrics.
4. `eval_model` L130-135 does one forward pass per impression. `get_news_embeddings` (a 512→50 linear, concat, then 250→50) is recomputed for the same news in every impression while the model is frozen. Computing all news embeddings once per eval and gathering them would remove that. `.detach()` inside `no_grad` is redundant. [M]
5. `save_embeddings` L151-152 runs without `torch.no_grad()`, building a graph over all users and all news. `write_embeddings` L160 then indexes `embeddings[index]` row by row on a tensor that requires grad (an autograd node per row) and calls `.tolist()` on each row. Detaching once and converting the whole tensor would avoid both. [M]
6. `read_bert_embeddings` L164-167 allocates an `np.zeros` float64 `[N,512]` array, and `torch.FloatTensor` then copies it to float32. Allocate float32 from the start. [F]
7. `read_bert_embeddings_from_file` L180 and L183 call `data_loader.news()` twice per line, and L182 builds a Python float list per line before assigning the row. `np.array(split, dtype=np.float32)` is cheaper. [F]

## news/src/python/train_mf.py
1. `train_epoch` L63 has the same `total_loss += loss` autograd chain. [M]
2. `train_model` L79-81 with `main` L145-146. With the default `epochs=100`, epoch 99 runs both evals and `main` immediately repeats them on the unchanged model. With `prob=1.0` the metrics are identical, so this is a full duplicate train and valid evaluation. [M]
3. `save_embeddings` L109-110 runs without `no_grad`. `model.user_embeddings(LongTensor(range(n)))` gathers a full copy of the weight matrix, where `.weight.detach()` would do. `write_embeddings` L118 indexes a grad tensor row by row. [M]
4. `train_model` L74 and `eval_model` L85 build feature tensors that are never used (see mind_data item 7).

## news/src/python/vespa_client.py and user_search.py
1. `query_user_embedding` L48 and `query_news` L67 use module-level `requests.get`/`requests.post`. Each call creates a new Session and connection, so every call pays a TCP handshake, plus an mTLS handshake on Vespa Cloud. news/evaluate.py makes 2 calls per impression, about 4,000 in total with the defaults. A module-level `requests.Session` fixes this. [N]
2. `query_news` L53-56 builds and joins a one-element list. Trivial.
3. user_search.py has nothing material.

## text-search/python/collect_training_data.py
The `msmarco` module imported at L7 does not exist in this repo. The only `load_msmarco_queries` is in extract-msmarco.py and has a different signature, so this script cannot run as checked in.
1. `build_dataset` L75 with `load_processed_queries` L63. `int(qid) not in processed_queries` tests membership in a list for every query, which is O(Q·P). Use a set. [P]
2. `build_dataset` L98-99. The append to `PROCESSED_QUERIES_FILE` sits at the loop level, outside the `if` at L75. On every resume, each query already processed is appended again, and the file is opened and closed once per query. The duplicates make the L75 scan longer on the next resume. [F]
3. `build_dataset` L92-97 calls `os.path.isfile` and then `DataFrame.from_records(...).to_csv(mode="a")` once per query, which reopens the file each time and pays pandas overhead per call. Keeping a `csv` writer open would be cheaper. [F]
4. `get_features` L38 uses `requests.post` without a session, so each of the 2 requests per query opens a new connection. [N]
5. `annotate_data` L53-55 creates three temporary single-key dicts for `update` and looks up `h["fields"]["id"]` twice. Trivial. [P]

## text-search/python/convert-to-vespa-format.py
1. `main` L62 uses `json.dump` per document, which is the pure-Python encoder. [F]
2. `main` L44-45 seeks once per document in the order of the offset file. That file is written from a set (sample-queries-and-documents.py L78), so the order is arbitrary and the reads are random seeks. Sorting by offset would make reads sequential but changes the output order. The gain on a page-cached file is unmeasured. [F]
3. `main` L43-44 iterates `keys()` and then indexes the dict. Trivial.

## text-search/python/create-sample-data.py (`<module>`)
1. L24-28 reads all qrels lines and splits every one to build a dict over all queries, then looks up 100 qids. Streaming and keeping only the lines whose qid is in `qids` gives the same result, provided the "last line wins" rule is kept. [F]
2. L35-38 reads the entire docs-lookup file with `readlines`, splits each line twice (`offset.split("\t")` appears twice in the comprehension), builds an intermediate list of tuples, and then builds the dict. [F]
3. L39-42 calls `random.sample(docids, …)` on a `dict_keys` view. On 3.10 that copies every key into a tuple on each call, and on 3.11 and later it raises. `list(docoffset)` built once gives the same order and the same sample. [P]

## text-search/python/extract-msmarco.py
1. `load_msmarco_queries` L26 calls `re.sub` with a string pattern for every query, which costs a cache lookup each time. Precompile it. The `qrel` parameter is unused, so every query is normalized, including those without judgements. [F]
2. `getcontent` L68-71 makes four `re.sub` calls per document with string patterns. Precompile the two patterns. Running the regexes over the body is unavoidable. [P]
3. `extract_documents` L84-86 does a seek and readline per document in lookup-table order (the code comment says the run takes about an hour). If that order matches the order of the file, a sequential read would avoid the seeks. I did not verify the order. [F]

## text-search/python/sample-queries-and-documents.py
1. `load_queries` L29 reapplies the regex and `lower()` that extract-msmarco.py already applied before writing queries.tsv (its L26 and L94). This is redundant. The second pass is idempotent except for possible Unicode `lower()` edge cases, which I did not check. [F]
2. `select_documents` L61-62 draws `random.choice` with replacement into a set until it reaches `min(len(docids), documents_to_generate)`. When the target is at least the corpus size (the default is 100000, against a small sample corpus), the loop has to collect every document, about n·ln n draws, just to return all ids. Returning `set(docids)` directly in that case gives the same set. The `min(...)` is also recomputed on every iteration. [P]

## msmarco-ranking/python
1. `evaluate_passage_run.py::eval` L103 with `main` L130-131. Sixteen worker threads share one Session whose HTTPAdapter has `pool_maxsize=10`. When more than 10 requests are in flight, urllib3 opens extra connections and discards them after use, so up to 6 threads keep paying new handshakes. Passing `pool_maxsize=16` fixes this. I inferred this from urllib3 behaviour and have not measured it. [N]
2. `evaluate_passage_run.py::get_result` L55-61 rescans the template dict for every query with `"{query}" in value`. Which keys need formatting never changes. Trivial. [P]
3. `evaluate_passage_run.py::eval_query` L91 checks `args.trec_format` for every hit. Trivial.
4. `to-vespa-feed.py::<module>` L19-20 calls `json.dump(doc, sys.stdout)` for every passage, which uses the pure-Python encoder with several writes, then makes a separate newline write. `sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(doc) + "\n")` is cheaper. [P, stdin/stdout]
5. `dump_passage_dev_qrels.py::<module>` has nothing material.

## scaling-tutorial/ext/transform_ms_marco.py (`<module>`)
1. L31-33 checks all 5 `SUBSETS` limits for every line, even after `i ≥ 500000` when only `"full"` can still match. Trivial. The `loads`/`dumps` round trip is needed. [F]

## multilingual-search/ext/evaluate.py
1. `search` L11-13 runs `iterrows()` over the group, building a Series per row, only to keep the last row's query. `query_group["query"].iloc[-1]` gets the same value. [P]
2. `main` L75 calls `groupby("query_id").apply(search)` purely for side effects, so pandas builds a sub-DataFrame per group. A plain loop over sorted rows would do the same, but it must keep groupby's sorted key order and the last-query-per-id rule. [P]

## colbert/model2onnx.py
1. `VespaColBERT.__init__` L16-18. `AutoModel.from_config` randomly initializes BERT, `self.init_weights()` initializes it again, and `from_pretrained` then overwrites the weights from the checkpoint. Newer transformers versions may skip most of this inside `no_init_weights`. I did not check the installed version. [M]

## colbert-long/scripts/convert.py
1. `remove_control_characters` L6-7 calls `unicodedata.category` in a Python loop over every character of every chunk in the corpus. A per-character cache or a `str.translate` table keeps the exact semantics, including the Cn category, while doing far fewer Python-level calls. [P]
2. `<module>` L23-24. `create_documents([text])` wraps each chunk in a langchain Document only for `.page_content` to be read back out, where `split_text(text)` returns the strings directly. langchain is not installed locally, so I could not inspect the per-chunk metadata copying inside `create_documents`. [P]
3. L24-25 make two list passes. Trivial.

## colbert-long/scripts/evaluate.py
1. `search` L26-29. A bare `except` reissues the request after the Session's `Retry(total=20)` has already retried, which only matters on the failure path. [N]
2. `search` L42 recomputes `str(query_id)` for every hit. Trivial.

## hypencoder
1. `encode_query.py::main` L70-72 converts a list of ints to a float32 array and back to a list, where `[float(i) for i in enc.ids]` gives the same result. It is 64 elements in a one-shot CLI, so negligible. [P]
2. `model2onnx.py::QueryEncoderWrapper._get_weights_and_biases_static` L106, L112, L117 and L123. `repeat_interleave(batch_size)` and `repeat(batch_size,1,1)` copy the query embeddings and base matrices per batch. These ops are traced into the exported ONNX graph, so they run on every query inside Vespa, where the batch is 1 and the copy buys nothing. A broadcast add for `hyper_base_matrices` would avoid copying a 768×768 matrix per query (the size comes from the comment at L143). I have not checked whether the hypencoder_cb attention accepts a broadcast query, and the runtime effect needs measuring in ONNX Runtime. [M]
3. The rest of model2onnx.py is one-shot export code with nothing material.

For local measurement, the best pure-ish candidates are:
- metrics.py
- `find_hit` and `predictions` in news/evaluate.py
- `MindData.add_entities`, `find_clicked` and `sample_valid_data` (construct an instance with `__new__`)
- `write_embedding`
- `remove_control_characters`
- `json.dump` against `json.dumps`
- the list-versus-set membership in collect_training_data.py
- `select_documents`

I have not measured any of these leads, so the size of each saving is unknown.
